::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[A group whose all elements are of order 1 or 2 is Abelian.](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2439220/a-group-whose-all-elements-are-of-order-1-or-2-is-abelian), asked by [John Mayne](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/311539/john-mayne) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2017-09-21; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> > Suppose you have $(G, \cdot)$a group whose all elements are either of order $1$ or $2$. Show that it's abelian.
>
> My proof, suppose you have $a,b \in G$ such that $a^1 = e$ and $b^1 =e$ then:  
> $$a \cdot b= e \cdot e = b \cdot a$$
>
> Now suppose we have $a^1 = e$ and $b^2 = e$:  
> $$a \cdot b = e \cdot b  = b \cdot e = b \cdot a$$
>
> And finally suppose $a^2 = e$ and $b^2 = e$ then:  
> $$a \cdot b = a \cdot ( a^{-1} \cdot a ) \cdot b = (a^{-1})(a^2)b=a^{-1}b$$
> and $$b \cdot a = b  (b^{-1} \cdot b ) a = b^{-1}(b^2)a = b^{-1}a$$
> Thus we have $$(a\cdot b)(b\cdot a)= (a^{-1} \cdot b)(b^{-1} \cdot a)= e$$
> Thus $ab=ba$. 
>
> Is my proof correct?
:::

Your first two cases are a little inelegant, since $a^1 = e$ means that $a=e$.  So the property that every element is of order 1 or 2 can be simplified to requiring $$x^2 = e,\; \forall  x \in G.$$

Here is a streamlined version.  Let $a, b \in G$ and let $x = ab$.  Since $x^2 = e$, we have
$$abab = e$$
Multiply on the right by $b$ and remember that $b^2 =e$ to get
$$aba = b$$
Multiply on the right by $a$ and remember that $a^2 =e$ to get
$$ab = ba$$
